prerequisiteEdges.justification: Simplifying is the inverse of generating equivalents and requires recognising the same multiplicative relationship.
Percent and decimal forms are equivalent fractions with denominators 100 or powers of ten, so the learner must first generate those equivalents.
Placing a fraction on a partitioned line uses the same equal-part reasoning that produces equivalent fractions.
A ratio is reduced to simplest integer parts by the same common-divisor process used to simplify a fraction.
Part–whole statements of a ratio are routinely written as fractions or percentages, so those conversions must already be fluent.
Sharing requires first knowing how many equal parts the whole has been partitioned into.
Applied modelling asks the learner to compute actual quantities once the ratio shares have been identified.
Diagrams and number-line models of mixes or lengths rely on correctly locating the rational shares.

misconceptions.label: Add numerators and denominators
misconceptions.description: Creates a new fraction by adding the two numerators and adding the two denominators instead of using a common multiplier or divisor.

misconceptions.label: Treat percent as a whole number
misconceptions.description: Writes 16 % as the integer 16 or as 16/1 rather than as 16/100 when converting among forms.

misconceptions.label: Read a:b as the single fraction a/b
misconceptions.description: Treats the ratio 2:3 as the fraction 2/3 of the whole, omitting the total of five parts.

items.stem: Write 16% as a fraction in simplest form.

options.rationale: 16% means 16 hundredths, so 16/100 simplifies by dividing numerator and denominator by 4.
Treats the percent as a whole number written over 1 instead of over 100.
Writes the percent as the integer 16 rather than as 16/100.

items.stem: A number line is marked from −2 to 3. Which point is at −1 1/2?

options.rationale: −1 1/2 lies midway between −2 and −1 on the number line.
That is the integer −1, one half-unit to the right of −1 1/2.
That is the positive mixed number, the reflection of the required point.

items.keyRationale: −1 1/2 is one and a half units left of zero, which is the midpoint of −2 and −1.

Rejected rather than repaired.

items.stem: A recipe uses flour and sugar in the ratio 2:3. How many equal parts is the mixture divided into?

options.rationale: The ratio 2:3 means 2 parts flour and 3 parts sugar, so 5 equal parts in total.
Reads only the first term of the ratio as the whole number of parts.
Treats the ratio as the single fraction 2/3 and takes the denominator as the number of parts.

items.keyRationale: A part–part ratio a:b has a + b equal parts altogether.

items.stem: Share $40 between Mia and Noah in the ratio 2:3. How much does Mia receive?

options.rationale: 2 + 3 = 5 parts; one part is $8; Mia’s 2 parts are $16.
Takes 2/3 of $40, treating the ratio as the single fraction 2/3 of the whole.
Gives Mia 3/5 of the money instead of 2/5.

items.keyRationale: Find the value of one part ($40 ÷ 5) then multiply by Mia’s 2 parts.

items.stem: A cordial mix uses 1 part concentrate to 4 parts water. How much concentrate is needed to make 750 mL of drink?

options.rationale: Uses 1:3 instead of 1:4, so four parts rather than five.
Takes one-third of 750 mL, as if the ratio were 1:2.
Gives the volume of water rather than the volume of concentrate.

items.keyRationale: Model the mix as 5 equal parts of 150 mL; one part is concentrate.
